strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP evaluation problem: measuring changes in social biases after continued masked-language-model training. Aligning the diagnostic with the model’s training objective is well motivated.

Retraining in both stereotype directions provides a useful intervention-based sanity check. Across four models and nine CrowS-Pairs categories, CRR, ΔP, and ΔPA consistently recover the expected direction in the reported experiments.

The paired comparisons, worked examples, and extensive category-level tables make the observed behavior inspectable. Evaluation on two established benchmarks and comparison with several existing measures provide useful empirical context.
weaknesses: The central claim of more accurate bias estimation is insufficiently validated. Appendix P.1 uses 80% of CrowS-Pairs for retraining, while the reported bias evaluation covers the full benchmark; most evaluated pairs therefore contain a training sentence. The expected retraining direction supplies the classification labels, and more extreme scores are treated as greater sensitivity without an independently established bias magnitude. Pair-disjoint evaluation and balanced or neutral retraining controls are needed to distinguish stereotype generalization from familiarity with the retraining sentences.

Human-annotation alignment provides weak independent support. Figures 4–5 show AUROCs of approximately 0.53–0.57, with small and inconsistent improvements over AUL/AULA. There are only 58 negative pairs versus 1,450 positive pairs, and no uncertainty estimates or significance tests for the differences. The description of thresholds that 'maximize' AUROC also needs clarification. Moreover, annotations of whether text expresses a stereotype do not directly establish how biased a model is.

The statistical evidence does not directly validate the reported BSRT changes or superiority between measures. McNemar’s test examines changes in binary sentence preferences, whereas Equation 10 measures whether the underlying preference gap increases. These are different quantities. More significant within-measure tests do not establish greater sensitivity between measures. Uncertainty estimates for the actual comparison statistic, direct paired comparisons between metrics, and variation across retraining seeds are needed.

Equation 10 mishandles ties under the stated interpretation. Comparing a model with itself gives BSRT = 0 because every strict inequality is false, yet Section 4.5.1 interprets scores below 50 as a directional bias change. The neutral reference point therefore requires explicit tie handling, particularly for rank-based measures that can produce identical scores.

The benefit of the new attention-weighted components is not isolated. CRRA changes both the rank transformation and attention weighting relative to CRR, so their effects are confounded. Unweighted ΔP already achieves perfect directional classification in this experiment, and attention does not consistently improve human-alignment results. Separate ablations are needed to substantiate the contribution of attention.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the supplied manuscript. Appendix P.1 omits the optimizer, learning rate, batch size, seeds, and exact data splits. Attention aggregation does not specify the layers, attention direction, and precise tensor reduction used. A released package is announced without a link or identifying reference. These omissions, together with the central validation concerns, warrant revision and resubmission next cycle before a clear Findings recommendation.
